COMMISSION PAYOUT UPON TERMINATION — STATEMENT OF EARNED BUT UNPAID COMMISSIONS
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

DECLARATION AND SCOPE OF THIS STATEMENT
This Statement of Earned but Unpaid Commissions is prepared by Jordan Lee, a former employee of Acme, Inc., whose employment ended on October 1, 2026. It identifies a commission that Jordan Lee contends was already earned, under the terms of the commission agreement between Jordan Lee and Acme, Inc., before employment ended — as distinct from a commission that was merely anticipated or still contingent on something that had not yet occurred as of October 1, 2026 — and that remains unpaid as of the date of this statement.

COMMISSIONS ARE "WAGES" UNDER CALIFORNIA LAW
California law defines "wages" to expressly include amounts computed on a commission basis, alongside amounts computed by time, task, or piece. Because an earned commission is legally a "wage" and not some separate, lesser category of pay, a commission that Jordan Lee actually earned while employed by Acme, Inc. is subject to the same statutory protections that apply to wages generally — including the final-pay-timing and waiting-time-penalty rules that already govern when other wages must be paid out at termination.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "“Wages” includes all amounts for labor performed by employees of every description, whether the amount is fixed or ascertained by the standard of time, task, piece, commission basis, or other method of calculation."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 200(a) (California Legislative Information text), the statutory definition of "wages" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=200.)
  "Section 200, subdivision (a) defines “wages” to include “all amounts for labor performed by employees of every description, whether the amount is fixed or ascertained by the standard of time, task, piece, commission basis, or other method of calculation.” (Italics added; see Reid v. Overland Machined Products (1961) 55 Cal.2d 203, 207-208 [commissions are wages].)"
  — Steinhebel v. Los Angeles Times Communications, LLC, 126 Cal. App. 4th 696, 704-705 (2005) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2259299/steinhebel-v-los-angeles-times-commun/)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that an earned commission is legally a "wage" — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific commission arrangement, and not a claim that other states classify commissions the same way. This clause cites a single statutory subsection (§ 200(a)); the second citation below is a California Court of Appeal decision quoting and applying that same subsection to commissions specifically, not an independent statutory source. This clause does not re-derive the final-pay-timing deadlines or the waiting-time-penalty mechanics themselves — this document set already contains dedicated, separately verified clauses covering those rules in full (in the Final Wage Payment / Waiting-Time Penalty Demand Letter document); this clause exists only to establish the threshold premise that an earned commission counts as a "wage" those rules reach in the first place.

THE COMMISSION-WRITING STATUTE SETS NO SEPARATE PAYOUT RULE FOR TERMINATION
The California statute that requires a commission arrangement to be in writing does not, on its own text, set out any separate rule for what happens to an unpaid commission when an employee's employment ends. Its requirements are about the writing itself — that the contract be in writing, that it state how commissions are computed and paid, that a signed copy be given to the employee, and that a signed receipt be obtained — not about a payout deadline or a special termination-triggered rule. Whether a specific commission was earned before October 1, 2026, and when an earned commission must be paid out once employment with Acme, Inc. ends, are questions this statute leaves to be answered elsewhere: by the commission agreement's own terms (which control what "earned" means) and by the general wage statutes that apply once a commission is properly classified as an earned wage.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(a) Whenever an employer enters into a contract of employment with an employee for services to be rendered within this state and the contemplated method of payment of the employee involves commissions, the contract shall be in writing and shall set forth the method by which the commissions shall be computed and paid. (b) The employer shall give a signed copy of the contract to every employee who is a party thereto and shall obtain a signed receipt for the contract from each employee. In the case of a contract that expires and where the parties nevertheless continue to work under the terms of the expired contract, the contract terms are presumed to remain in full force and effect until the contract is superseded or employment is terminated by either party. (c) As used in this section, “commissions” has the meaning set forth in Section 204.1."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2751 (California Legislative Information text), the full written-commission-contract statute, subsections (a) through (c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2751.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of what this specific statutory section does and does not address — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific commission arrangement. This clause makes a negative claim (that § 2751 contains no termination-specific default rule); that negative claim was checked by reading the section's full text directly rather than assumed, and the full text of subsections (a) through (c) is what supports it. This document deliberately does not re-derive the written-contract, signed-copy, signed-receipt, or expired-contract-continuation requirements of this same statute in general, since this document set already contains dedicated, separately verified clauses covering each of those (in the Commission Agreement document); this clause exists only to make clear, for a reader assembling this specific termination-focused document, that this well-known commission statute does not itself supply a termination payout rule, so one should not be inferred from it.

WHAT MAKES A COMMISSION "EARNED": THE CONDITION-PRECEDENT DISTINCTION
California courts have held that a commission is not automatically "earned," as a matter of law, simply because the underlying sale or transaction that will eventually generate it has occurred. An employer may lawfully condition an employee's right to a commission on a further contingency — something in addition to the sale itself — and until that contingency actually occurs, the commission is not yet an earned wage. A payment made to the employee before the contingency occurs is legally an advance, not a wage, precisely because the employer cannot yet determine whether the commission will ever actually be earned. Whether a specific commission that Jordan Lee points to was actually earned before October 1, 2026, or was instead still subject to an unsatisfied contingency as of that date, depends on what the commission agreement between Jordan Lee and Acme, Inc. itself identifies as the condition for earning it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The essence of an advance is that at the time of payment the employer cannot determine whether the commission will eventually be earned because a condition to the employee’s right to the commission has yet to occur or its occurrence as yet is otherwise unascertainable. An advance, therefore, by definition is not a wage because all conditions for performance have not been satisfied."
  — Steinhebel v. Los Angeles Times Communications, LLC, 126 Cal. App. 4th 696, 705-706 (2005) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2259299/steinhebel-v-los-angeles-times-commun/)
  "In the present case, under the stipulated facts, appellants’ commission was contingent upon two general conditions... Unless both conditions were met, there was no “commissionable sale.” Appellants’ commissions were predicated on a successful sale, and unless a sale met both conditions, there was in fact no sale."
  — Steinhebel v. Los Angeles Times Communications, LLC, 126 Cal. App. 4th 696, 705 (2005) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2259299/steinhebel-v-los-angeles-times-commun/)
  Known gap: This is one state's case law, used as real evidence of how California courts have drawn the earned-versus-contingent line for commissions — not a claim about which state's law governs this particular commission arrangement, and not a claim that any particular contingency in any particular agreement is enforceable. THE COMMISSION AGREEMENT'S OWN TERMS CONTROL WHAT COUNTS AS "EARNED"
California courts have held that there is no single, universal legal trigger — such as the date of the sale, the date of a customer's order, or the date of a customer's payment — that automatically determines when a commission is "earned" in every case. Instead, an employee's right to a commission is governed by whatever the commission agreement between the employee and the employer itself specifies as the earning trigger. This is why the method-of-computation-and-payment language in a written commission agreement, of the kind California law already separately requires be in writing, is central to answering whether a particular commission was earned before October 1, 2026: 5% of net sales revenue, earned upon the customer's countersignature of the contract, paid on the next regular payday

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Appellants’ right to commissions therefore must be governed by the provisions of the Agreement. ... “[T]he right of a salesman or any other person to commissions under given circumstances depends upon the terms of his contract for compensation.” (Commeford, at p. 118.)"
  — Steinhebel v. Los Angeles Times Communications, LLC, quoting Commeford v. Baker, 127 Cal.App.2d 111, 118 (1954), 126 Cal. App. 4th 696, 705 (2005) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2259299/steinhebel-v-los-angeles-times-commun/)

This clause quotes a passage from Commeford v. ONCE A COMMISSION IS ACTUALLY EARNED, IT CANNOT BE TAKEN BACK AS A WAGE
Separately from the question of when a commission becomes earned in the first place, California law makes it unlawful for an employer to collect or receive back any part of wages it has already paid an employee. California courts have read this rule together with the earned-versus-contingent distinction described elsewhere in this document: an employer may lawfully make an earlier payment contingent on something not yet satisfied (so that no wage has been earned yet), but once a commission has actually been earned by the employee's completion of everything the agreement required for it to be earned, that protection against employers clawing back already-paid wages applies to it like any other wage.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "It shall be unlawful for any employer to collect or receive from an employee any part of wages theretofore paid by said employer to said employee."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 221 (California Legislative Information text), the prohibition on collecting back wages already paid (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=221.)
  "In referring to “wages” paid, section 221 prohibits an employer only from collecting or receiving wages that have already been earned by performance of agreed-upon requirements."
  — Steinhebel v. Los Angeles Times Communications, LLC, 126 Cal. App. 4th 696, 707 (2005) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2259299/steinhebel-v-los-angeles-times-commun/)

This clause cites a single statutory section (§ 221) and a single Court of Appeal decision applying it to a commission chargeback scheme; the case addressed an advance-and-chargeback arrangement where the court found no wage had yet been earned (so § 221 was not implicated), not a case where an employer took back a commission the court found to be already earned — so this clause states the general principle the court articulated rather than an outcome directly forfeiting an earned commission. Basis, under the commission agreement between Jordan Lee and Acme, Inc., for treating this amount as already earned rather than still contingent as of October 1, 2026: 5% of net sales revenue, earned upon the customer's countersignature of the contract, paid on the next regular payday
